entries.title: Focus group invites sent to White Sox fans as part of Justin Isbhia's South Loop stadium proposal
entries.summary: <p>Some White Sox fans received an interesting email on Friday afternoon.</p><p>The message invoked public reports of “future White Sox owner Justin Ishbia’s vision for a new, state-of-the-art ballpark,” and invited fans to RSVP for “a limited number of in-person focus group sessions” early next month to give feedback on “potential ballpark features, seating experiences, and overall game-day enhancements” for the proposed new stadium.</p><p>The emails also had a White Sox logo at the top, and all the legal language of an MLB-approved message at the bottom.</p><p>But despite the appearances, the Sox indicate they are just acting as mailmen. The focus groups are being held by Ishbia’s City River Holdings venture, which has been working to develop <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/10/28/bridgeport-bears-domed-stadium-proposal-sox-rate-field" target="_blank" ><u>a mixed-use district in the South Loop with the proposed title of “The Railyards”</u></a> that will house a new White Sox stadium. Rather than hand over customer contact info to a third party, the team is assisting by sending the emails themselves.</p><p>“When we announced the vision for The Railyards in September, we said this was the beginning of a multi-year planning and approval process, and this is part of that process,” a spokesperson for Ishbia explained in an email.</p><p>The feedback received from these groups could affect future stadium proposals, or be used to demonstrate the public support level for the project.</p><p>These invites hit the inboxes of Sox fans at the end of a week that brought word of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/26/amtraks-bridgeport-railyard-to-get-environmental-review-after-community-pressure-lets-keep-up-the-fight" target="_blank" ><u>Amtrak’s proposed new facility in Bridgeport undergoing a federal environmental review</u></a>, after months of pressure from neighborhood residents. The proposal is a corresponding effort with Ishbia’s plans to develop the site of Amtrak’s current facility into the Sox’ future home. The team’s current lease with Bridgeport’s Rate Field runs through the 2029 season, which is also the first year that Ishbia’s ownership transfer agreement with current chairman Jerry Reinsdorf could see the former take control of the franchise.</p><p>Until then, all White Sox business is to remain under the current chairman’s purview. As such, it would have been surprising to see the club sending out official emails embracing Ishbia’s future plans. Instead, everyone involved says the Sox are just acting as the messenger.</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: New faces at new places in high school boys basketball
entries.summary: <p>There wasn’t a whole lot of turnover in the basketball coaching carousel this past offseason. But there were a few intriguing spots to be filled.</p><p>Here is a closer look at several new coaches who will be leading six of the bigger programs in the area this season.</p><p>Glenbard North<br><b>Former coach: </b>Kevin Tonn<br><b>New coach: </b>Nick Healy</p><p>After leading the Panthers to 24 wins and DuKane Conference and regional championships, Tonn felt the pull of his alma mater and took the Wheaton North job.</p><p>Now Healy, the son of Wheaton South head coach Mike Healy and most recently an assistant at Waubonsie Valley, takes over a team that could be ranked in the preseason with four returning starters. That strong nucleus includes the talented 1-2 punch of 6-3 Lamari Carpenter and 6-6 Oturo Redento.</p><p>Lake Park<br><b>Former coach: </b>Billy Pitcher<br><b>New coach: </b>Bob Reibel</p><p>Reibel crosses over from coaching Lake Park’s girls program, where he won both DuKane Conference and regional titles while setting a program record for wins, to lead the boys. He has been the girls coach for the last three seasons.</p><p>Reibel inherits some exciting players, including 6-6 Brennan Shannon and sophomores Christian Burge and Frank Battaglia.</p><p>Oswego East<br><b>Former coach: </b>Ryan Velasquez<br><b>New coach: </b>Brian Johnson</p><p>Oswego East basketball enjoyed a terrific nine-year run under Velasquez, who stepped down after going 198-71 and winning 20-plus games every season except for the Covid-shortened one.</p><p>The search for a coach landed on one with experience. Johnson led West Aurora for eight years and Kaneland for six. Johnson, who most recently was an assistant coach at Metea Valley, won four regionals and a sectional title in 2018 while at West Aurora.</p><p>St. Viator<br><b>Former coach: </b>Michael O’Keefe<br><b>New coach: </b>Al Biancalana</p><p>There isn’t a new coach with more experience than Biancalana.</p><p>The veteran coach has 25 years of head-coaching experience, including stints at Glenbard East, DeKalb, York and Stagg. He also was a Division I assistant at Bradley and UIC for 10 years. Most recently, Biancalana has spent the last four years as Mike Bailey’s assistant at St. Patrick.</p><p>While there were departures and turnover in the program, Biancalana does have veteran returner Dawson Charles to build around in Year 1. He averaged 19.2 points last season as a junior.</p><p>Cary-Grove<br><b>Former coach: </b>Adam McCloud<br><b>New coach: </b>Christian Spandiary</p><p>There were a couple of highs over McCloud’s 10-year run as coach, including last year’s conference championship team that won 28 games. The 2019-20 season produced a school-record 31 wins and a regional title.</p><p>Now Spandiary takes over. As a former star player at Schaumburg and assistant coach at Barrington, Spandiary brings his Mid-Suburban League roots to the Fox Valley Conference. He takes over a team that lost all five starters.</p><p>Schaumburg<br><b>Former coach: </b>Jason Tucker<br><b>New coach: </b>Garett Gatz</p><p>Gatz takes over a program after five years as an assistant, including the last four as the sophomore coach. Before his time at Schaum-<br>burg, Gatz worked under highly successful Conant coach Tom McCormack, now retired, who he also played for in high school.</p><p>The Saxons, who have very little returning from a year ago, have just one regional championship in the last 14 years.</p>
entries.author: Joe Henricksen

entries.title: Patrick Williams' contract status carries no weight with Bulls regime
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON – The groin injury that sidelined Patrick Williams the last week was in the past. His days of being a continual DNP (Did Not Play) Coach’s Decision were not.</p><p>That doesn’t mean Bulls coach Tiago Splitter doesn’t see value in the No. 4 overall pick from the 2020 draft, letting him know to stay ready. Staying ready, however, and seeing playing time as a rotation piece are two very different conversations.</p><p>“I told him during the whole camp and before we started the games he was doing a great job, he was forcing his hand and making my life difficult because he was doing a good job,” Splitter said on Friday. “He’s got to stay ready. His moment is going to come. You can’t just switch rotations every day. You’ve got to stick to something and evaluate, see how the young guys are doing. He’s going to have time to play and there will be changes made throughout the season, so he’s ready to go.”</p><p>Unfortunately for Williams there’s a handful of players in front of him that are not only ready to go but have proven more with this new coaching staff. Rookie Caleb Wilson and Matas Buzelis are the starting forwards, while Isaac Okoro, Leonard Miller and Noa Essengue are the backup forwards Splitter has been using.</p><p>That line Williams is waiting in is only about to get longer when Nic Claxton (hamstring) is able to make his Bulls debut. That means Jalen Smith becomes the back-up five/four, adding to the logjam in the frontcourt.</p><p>And yes, Williams might be the highest paid of all that group at $18 million a year through the 2028-29 season in which he will undoubtedly pick up his player option, but that has no influence with the new front office or coaching staff.</p><p>Splitter was asked if there had been any conversations with executive vice president of basketball operations Bryson Graham in which the coach was told that Williams had to be looked at for minutes just because of the contract he was carrying, and Splitter replied, “No, we never had that conversation.”</p><p></p><p><b>Crafty veteran</b></p><p></p><p>Okoro doesn’t need to be reminded that he is in the final year of a deal in which he makes $11.8 million this season, admitting that it’s not something that weighs on his mind or influences the way he takes the court each night.</p><p>Yes, he can be a valuable trade asset come February if the front office wants to move him but his mindset was that’s a concern for another day.</p><p>“It’s my seventh year in the league,” Okoro said. “I know what comes with it. I know every time I step on the court I’ve got to play my game. I have to do what I do best. There’s no, ‘Oh it’s a contract year so I’ve got to go out and shoot 10 threes a game, I’ve got to be ball dominant.’ Like no, I’ve been in the league this long being who I’ve been. So anytime I step on the court it’s about playing hard, being competitive, try and lead the team the way I can. You got to focus on the Chicago Bulls and how can we get wins, how can we get better.”</p><p></p><p><b>Training room</b></p><p></p><p>Rookie Dailyn Swain was unavailable against Boston, dealing with soreness, according to Splitter.</p><p>“We decided to not have him playing, nothing serious,” Splitter said of Swain, who was not in the rotation mix anyway this season.</p><p>Claxton continued ramping up his activity during the morning shootaround and the hope remained getting him in practices on this current road trip.</p>

entries.title: Lake View hospital kitchen reopens after license pulled for 'cockroach infestation,' other violations
entries.summary: <p>Illinois Masonic Medical Center's cafeteria and kitchen has reopened after it was shuttered earlier this month when a “cockroach infestation” contributed to a failed health inspection, according to the Chicago Department of Public Health.</p><p>The kitchen had its license suspended Oct. 16 for failing the inspection, and multiple citations were issued, but it was reinstated Thursday after a follow-up inspection, the department said in a statement Friday.</p><p>In the report published earlier this month, city inspectors said they observed more than 200 live cockroaches in multiple areas, which included food preparation areas, the grill and deep fryer areas, dry storage and the main dish room, per <a class="Link" href="https://data.cityofchicago.org/Health-Human-Services/Food-Inspections/4ijn-s7e5/data_preview" target="_blank" ><u>city records</u></a>. Dead roaches were found under the dry storage racks for a second time after staff were instructed to clean them during an inspection earlier this year.</p><p>It also detailed black slime accumulating inside a cooler until it dripped onto ice being used for the cafeterias. Inspectors also observed utensils being improperly stored, old food on walls and a mounted can opener. There were leaky pipes and accumulations of dust, grease, and dirt throughout the kitchen and storage areas. </p><p>Other previous violations were also said to have not been corrected.</p><p>The follow-up inspection shows the hospital had exterminators at the premises and remedied all other violations, according to city documents. Advocate Health, which operates Illinois Masonic, didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>The Rendezvous Cafeteria and patient kitchen at the hospital passed an inspection with conditions April 15. City officials noted the dead cockroaches in the dry storage area and said the kitchens were storing raw chicken above 56 degrees and other foods at similarly high temperatures. A manager, the inspection said, disposed of $250 in food on the spot, though citations were still issued.</p><p>The hospital’s Ecos Cafe also faced citations for storing food at high temperatures and having the handwashing sink in its prep area obstructed by clutter, among other issues, per a separate April 15 report. In that case, employees disposed of nine pounds of food that inspectors had marked as improperly stored.</p><p>It's the fifth time since 2010 that a kitchen at the hospital has failed a health inspection, per city records.</p><p>The hospital last failed a city inspection in August 2023, when inspectors once noted the buildup of black slime in the ice machines and on food — such as salmon and chicken — being stored at improperly high temperatures, per the report.</p>

entries.title: Inspired by Frank Lloyd Wright then wronged by neglect, South Park Terrace heads for auction
entries.summary: <p>A picturesque 121-year-old South Side courtyard building inspired by an historic Frank Lloyd Wright design — and featured in a 1995 Halle Berry movie — is now scheduled for auction.</p><p>South Park Terrace, a Prairie School-styled apartment building at 6116 S. King Drive, is set to be auctioned off Nov. 16-18, according to a marketing brochure by Frontline Real Estate Partners.</p><p>The opening bid is $100,000. </p><p>"We do expect it to go for significantly more than that," Frontline Principal Matthew Tarshis said.</p><p>Frontline was named South Park Terrace's court-appointed receiver, after the building was vacated under city order in 2025 due to its dilapidated condition.</p><p>Officials saw the situation as exigent enough that residents had to begin leaving the building with just two days notice.</p><p>The city’s Department of Buildings said in a statement at the time that the owners, listed then as Brooklyn, New York’s 6116 MLK, “completely abandoned the building, allowing the property to go into foreclosure, and conditions continued to deteriorate to the point of imminent danger to the community.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure King Dr. is boarded up after tenants were told in 2025 to vacate the premises.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Frontline's 14-page marketing brochure touts the location of the two-story, 52-unit Washington Park building and its notable, park-like private courtyard.</p><p>South Park Terrace is on a major public transit route, is two blocks from a CTA Green Line stop and near the jobs-rich University of Chicago and medical complex.</p><p>Preservation Chicago placed South Park Terrace on its 2026 list of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/03/04/art-institute-expansion-louis-sullivan-chicago-stock-exchange" >Chicago’s seven most endangered places</a>, but there's cause for relief: The building is not being marketed as a tear-down.</p><p>"We believe that the highest and best use for the property is for somebody to come in, and hopefully inject fresh capital, renovate the property, and ideally lease it up and stabilize it," Tarshis said.</p><p>Me too.</p><p>What a great building. And its close to the Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvery Vaux-designed Washington Park and near more amenities and employment opportunities than you can shake a stick at.</p><p>And shame on every entity — public and private — that let such well-designed, affordably priced housing fall into ruin. If any building deserves a second chance, it’s this one.</p><p>Built in 1905 for developer Thomas E. Wells — you can see his initials molded into terra cotta medallions on the building’s entry arch — South Park Terrace was designed by Harry Hale Waterman, an associate of Frank Lloyd Wright.</p><p>In the 1995 film “Losing Isaiah," Halle Berry’s character, Khaila Richards, lives in the building. The exterior and the courtyard are prominently seen in the movie.</p><p>Waterman patterned the building after Wright’s Francisco Terrace Apartments, built in 1895 at 253-257 N. Francisco Ave.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-eb0000" name="image-eb0000"></a> Digital File #67365</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Wells must have liked the design: He hired architect Douglas S. Pentecost to give South Park Terrace a twin, Washington Park Terrace, which was built in 1909 and still stands at 6160-6212 S. King Drive.</p><p>The three buildings sought to give natural light, fresh air, greenery and good design to their working class tenants — a mission that’s as important now as it was 120 years ago. Maybe more so.</p><p>Francisco Terrace was wrecked in 1974. It’s time to make sure the same fate doesn’t befall South Park Terrace. It needs a buyer who won’t let demolition by neglect happen somewhere down the road, or alter the building in some way that diminishes its beauty and importance.</p><p>Given South Park Terrace's design and pedigree, a city and the landmark commission must soon consider a designation that would protect the main elevations and courtyard.</p><p>Maybe a two-for-the-price-of-one deal that also includes its street mate, Washington Park Terrace.</p><p>While we're at it, the city would also do a lot of good by stepping in after the sale and working with the new owners to keep rents in the building affordable for working class folk.</p><p>Preservation Chicago Executive Director Ward Miller said, "We are hopeful that a new good steward would come forward to purchase and restore this amazing building."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2025/06/19/endangered-washington-park-building-frank-lloyd-wright-rescue" >Washington Park building inspired by Frank Lloyd Wright is in need of rescue</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Eshun Flowers' punt-block TD sparks Simeon to a 6A playoff win over Oak Lawn
entries.summary: <p>Simeon's youngsters had to grow up in a hurry, and they did.</p><p>The Wolverines ran a gauntlet of tough teams to open the season, losing their first three games and five of their first six. But Simeon survived and has won five in a row, the latest 28-19 over host Oak Lawn Friday night in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/10/17/ihsa-state-football-playoff-pairings-class6a-illinois-2026" >Class 6A</a> first round.</p><p>"We had everybody putting us down, just giving up on us," sophomore quarterback Aki King said. "We ain't give up on ourselves. That was the main thing. We just went out there, kept fighting."</p><p>They did it once more against Oak Lawn, rallying from a 13-6 deficit with three straight scores.</p><p>The last came on the first play of the fourth quarter when sophomore Eshun Flowers blocked a Spartans punt, scooped it up and ran 25 yards for a touchdown to give Simeon (6-5) a 28-13 lead.</p><p>"Oh, that was wonderful," said Simeon junior Bryce Kidd, who ran for one TD and caught a pass for another. "That was the game-sealer, right there."</p><p>Earlier, King threw a 25-yard TD pass to Kidd and Kidd raced 79 yards down the right sideline for another score.</p><p>Running back James Bell, one of the state's top uncommitted seniors, added an eight-yard TD run for the Wolverines, who play next week against Nazareth or Dunlap.</p><p>King ran seven times for 55 yards and was 4-of-9 passing for 57 yards as Oak Lawn (7-3) built its defensive game plan around containing the pass-and-catch duo of King and fellow soph Jalonny Billingsley.</p><p>"That's why we try to use our tendencies to our advantage in certain situations and whatnot, knowing that J5 [Billingsley] is going to get a lot of attention," Simeon coach Sinque Turner said. "And we've got a kid that's a track star [Kidd] that we can get the ball to, and he can make some of the same [or] similar plays as Jalonny."</p><p>King, meanwhile, has grown into his role after those early losses.</p><p>"Just by him going through the things he's been going through over these last 12, 11 games or whatnot, he's gained a lot of experience against a lot of top competition," Turner said. "So he's matured drastically. ... Still a lot of growing to do, but nonetheless, I think the sky's the limit for that kid."</p><p>King is seeing the reward for the work he put in over the offseason, with Kidd and the rest of his receivers.</p><p>"We've been [doing] seven-on-seven with each other for a year and some change now," King said. "[Kidd is] just a dog, track style. He gets in. the open field, he ain't getting caught."</p><p>After Flowers' touchdown, Simeon's defense stepped up with a pair of fumble recoveries and a fourth-down stop at its own two-yard line. Oak Lawn scored with 1:25 left, but missed the extra point and the Wolverines ran out the clock.</p><p>Jayden Schlosser ran 23 times for 134 yards and a pair of touchdowns for Oak Lawn. Quarterback Danny Strelow also ran for a short score.</p><p>The Spartans have won seven games two years in a row after 15 straight losing seasons, including an 0-9 finish in 2024.</p><p>"These seniors, they were a special group," Oak Lawn Ryan Pattison said. "They were a big part of turning around this program last year ... and then this year. ... They just wanted to leave this place better than they found it. And they did that."</p>

entries.title: Little-known Goode entertains the state in 88-84 playoff loss to Quincy played at two different fields
entries.summary: <p>Goode is one of the newer high schools in Chicago. It opened in 2012 and started up a football program in 2014. Few people have even heard of the school. Until Friday. </p><p>Goode played an astounding Class 6A state playoff game against visiting Quincy. The Knights lost 88-84 in a game that started at 3 p.m., lasted four hours, set multiple state records, and had to be moved to a second high school when darkness set in. Goode's field does not have lights. </p><p>“Survive and advance. I am proud to say we did that tonight,” Quincy coach Rick Little told the WGEM streaming broadcast following the game. “I am proud of this team and their resolve.”</p><p>Chicago Public Schools scheduled the game for 3 p.m. on Saturday at Rockne Stadium. But since Quincy didn't have school on Friday they asked Goode if the teams could play the game on Friday afternoon. Goode agreed. </p><p>The fireworks arrived as soon as the game started and Goode led 60-59 at halftime. The halftime break was shortened to six minutes. Officials were worried about the impending darkness. </p><p>The game was suspended at 5:50 p.m. with Quincy ahead 88-84 and 3:42 left to play. Everyone headed over to Englewood high school to finish the game. </p><p>Play restarted at 6:53 p.m. </p><p>Quincy quarterback Bryson Little threw a state single-game record eight touchdown passes and rushed for two TDs.</p><p>The combined 172 points are the most-ever in a high school game in Illinois, topping the 166 set scored when Springfield beat Rock Island 94-72 on October 29, 2021.</p><p>“This is why we love high school sports,” IHSA Executive Director Craig Anderson said. “The circumstances weren’t ideal, but everyone involved came together on behalf of students, and the result is something that no one involved with this game is ever going to forget. I encourage anyone reading this to go support a local high school event this weekend. Whether it is another football playoff game, a Sectional Championship soccer match, or a Sectional Cross Country meet. You may not see as many records fall as you did in the Quincy-Goode game, but what you will see is the epitome of education-based athletics: young people giving everything they have while representing their schools and communities.”<br></p>
entries.author: Michael O'Brien

entries.title: Intense, underrated Oklahoma State recruit TJ Lewis powers Bolingbrook past Lockport
entries.summary: <p>Bolingbrook senior TJ Lewis runs so hard in practice that his coach, Titcus Pettigrew, worries it might get dangerous.</p><p>‘‘We have to take him out sometimes,’’ Pettigrew said. ‘‘The intensity. And the defense doesn’t let up. Someone is going to injure someone with how hard he runs and how hard they hit. It is just his passion. He has a big chip on his shoulder. And he has some big shoulders.’’</p><p>Lewis says that chip on his shoulder is because national recruiting websites have underrated him.</p><p>‘‘I’m ranked No. 32 in Illinois right now [by 247Sports.com], which is not true,’’ Lewis said. ‘‘They can see it like that. But my play is going to get me where we need to be.’’</p><p>Lewis ran for 182 yards and three touchdowns to lead the No. 7 Raiders to a 38-14 rout of visiting Lockport in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/10/17/ihsa-state-football-playoff-pairings-class8a-illinois-2026" target="_blank" >Class 8A</a> first-round playoff game <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/10/30/2026-ihsa-state-football-first-round-playoff-scores" target="_blank" >Friday</a>.</p><p>‘‘If they want to keep doubting that boy and not give him his flowers, I say thank you,’’ Pettigrew said. ‘‘I want to keep it that way because it keeps him motivated.’’</p><p>Lewis has committed to Oklahoma State, and 247Sports.com lists him as the No. 2 running back in the state.</p><p>‘‘I was afraid we would not be able to tackle him,’’ Porters coach George Czart said. ‘‘The plan was to make sure we went low on him. If you try to tackle him up high, he is just going to shake you off. He’s so strong with his core. Even that didn’t work. You have to get as many guys as you can on him. He did such a great job of cutting and finding a hole. He’s so explosive through the hole. Anything we tried to do didn’t work.’’</p><p>Lewis scored on a 32-yard run on his first touch of the game. It was Bolingbrook’s first offensive play after Lockport (6-5) threw an interception on its opening drive.</p><p>The Raiders (9-1) led 24-7 at halftime, and Lewis scored on a 24-yard run early in the third quarter to make it 31-7.</p><p>‘‘TJ is a dog,’’ Bolingbrook defensive lineman Darieon Prescott said. ‘‘I’m so proud of how he’s grown up as a player and a person.’’</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: Rookie Caleb Wilson blasts Bulls, self after blowout loss in Boston
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON – There was actually a hint of enthusiasm in Josh Giddey’s voice.</p><p>The Bulls guard was standing in the visiting locker room of Boston’s TD Garden on Monday, discussing the pending rematch just a few days later.</p><p>“We get another chance at these guys so it will be good to see how we respond,” Giddey insisted after that 134-99 drubbing.</p><p>Response seen.</p><p>Everyone, cover your eyes.</p><p>For the second time in a five-day period, the rebuilding Bulls (1-5) strolled into TD Garden with high hopes only to see them thrown to the ground, stomped on and discarded with the other trash left on the court. It was another uncompetitive night against the Celtics, a 125-111 romp. And the first game of pool play in the NBA Cup wasn’t even that close.</p><p>Rookie Caleb Wilson called out everything, including the effort and himself.</p><p>“I’m 20, and I’ve never been a loser in my whole life, so I’m going to try my best to make sure that doesn’t happen, and I’m not ever going to accept being a loser,” Wilson said of trying to will the team back into it in the second half. “This is my job, to be a leader on this team, and it’s all going to start with me. I know that. It’s partially my fault that we started off the way we did, whether I’m the youngest on the team or not. I take ownership for that, and it won’t happen again.”</p><p>Boston (4-1) put on a clinic in every facet of the game from the opening tip Friday, outscoring the Bulls 44-25 in the first quarter.</p><p>The Celtics outscored the Bulls 24-10 in the paint and outshot them 67% to 32% from the field, and their bench put up 22 points compared to the Bulls second unit’s measly four in the first quarter.</p><p>It was disappointing, considering the Bulls were looking forward to seeing how they would respond against a top-tier team in the East, but even more so because they had just played one of their better games Wednesday against the defending NBA champion Knicks.</p><p>Lesson learned: Momentum in a rebuild is just a three-syllable word.</p><p>“I know our team doesn’t have superstars like Jayson Tatum and Paul George, but we’re young, and that’s going to be our advantage all year,” Wilson said. “If we’re not going to play hard, it’s not going to work. We’re going to lose every game. We’re all young; we shouldn’t be letting anyone play harder than us.”</p><p>Wilson wasn’t the only one who had something to say after a second-half play in which Payton Pritchard snatched a rebound from Matas Buzelis, knocking him to the ground, then seconds later took advantage of a Bulls turnover with a three-pointer. Buddy Hield was vocal on the bench with his teammates during the timeout.</p><p>“Buddy was just saying that we needed to have some type of pride and passion, and I agree with it, for sure,” Wilson said. “I mean, we’re the Chicago Bulls. I feel like it’s unacceptable to be looking like we are and also be laying down that early in the game.”</p><p>Wilson had 23 points, including six three-pointers, five rebounds and four assists.</p><p>But the game was disappointing overall, especially defensively, where it looked like strides were being made.</p><p>“My motto is always day-by-day,” Isaac Okoro said of the defense. “I can see us starting to be more physical, picking up full court, getting into the ball more as the game goes on because everybody is preaching it just more and more. That doesn’t mean it’s where it needs to be at all.”</p>
